name: Agreement with the Shoshone of September 26, 1872 (the Brunot cession)
citation: Agreement of September 26, 1872, ratified by Act of December 15, 1874, 18 Stat. 291
nations: Eastern Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation
promises: The Shoshone ceded, subject to the approval of Congress, the part of their 1868 reservation south of a line from the eastern boundary along the Little Popo Agie and the Popo Agie to the mouth of the canyon and west to the boundary (Royce schedule).
They kept the rest of the reservation, the present Wind River reservation (Royce schedule).
The United States agreed to spend $5,000 a year for five years for their use and to pay Chief Washakie $500 a year for five years (ICC findings).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the Brunot lands were worth eighty cents an acre, or $560,513.60, on September 26, 1872, and held that the $27,500 paid, under four cents an acre, was an unconscionable consideration.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Shoshone Tribe of Indians of the Wind River Reservation v. United States, Docket 63, 3 Ind. Cl. Comm. 313 and 333 (1954)

source.title: Shoshone Tribe of Indians of the Wind River Reservation v. United States, Docket 63, Opinion of the Commission (3 Ind. Cl. Comm. 333, August 20, 1954)
source.publisher: Indian Claims Commission Decisions, Oklahoma State University Library

breaches.quote: purchase price of less than four cents per acre for lands worth twenty times that amount

landTaken: The 1872 agreement described 700,642 acres, as both parties agreed before the Commission (Docket 63 findings and opinion).
compensation: Value $560,513.60 against $27,500 paid; the 1954 interlocutory order awarded $533,013.60 less offsets. The parties later agreed offsets of $100,000, and the Commission entered a final order on April 22, 1957 (1958 opinion, Docket 63).
today: A separate claim (Docket 157) that white miners invaded the reservation between 1868 and 1874 and removed large quantities of gold, for which the petitioner held the United States responsible, was settled by compromise in 1965 for a judgment of $120,000 (a stipulated gold value of $195,000 less $75,000 in offsets).

nationVoice.summary: The tribe writes that after the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty, later agreements ceded the South Pass and Big Horn Hot Springs regions, leaving about 2.2 million acres.

openQuestions: treaties.json error: this record names the "Sioux, Wahpeton" (scheduleTribes) and the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate (presentDayTribes). Royce's September 26, 1872 entry (area 539, Wyoming) is the Shoshone agreement; presentDayTribes should be the Eastern Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation.

The final award figure of April 22, 1957 is partly unreadable in the 1958 opinion scan; value less price less the $100,000 offsets would be $433,013.60, which matches the readable digits but was left out of the record.
The government argued the 1868 treaty had reserved only about 503,000 of the 700,642 acres; the Commission rejected this.

Audit 2026-11-08: today corrected: Docket 157 alleged gold taken between 1868 and 1874 (not 'between 1868 and the cession') and that the United States was responsible (not 'with United States help'); the $120,000 settlement figure added (OSU id 883). The $533,013.60 interlocutory figure is stated in the 1958 opinion (OSU id 322). Royce's September 26, 1872 entry has two areas: 539 is the ceded southern part (this record) and 540 is the retained Wind River reservation, which treaties.json files as cession-1872-09-26-shoshoni; that record uses the same Docket 63 finding for land that was not ceded.

plain.promised: In 1872 the Eastern Shoshone gave up the southern part of their Wind River reservation, where miners had moved in. The United States agreed to spend $5,000 a year for five years for them and pay Chief Washakie $500 a year.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1954 that the land was worth $560,513.60 and that the $27,500 paid, under four cents an acre, was unconscionable.
plain.today: After $100,000 in offsets the Commission entered a final order in 1957. A separate claim for gold taken by miners was settled in 1965.
